Medicaid Work Requirements 2027: Will You Lose Coverage? By ModernWallet Research Desk · Reviewed by Jonathan Teplitsky, MBA · Updated November 25, 2026 · How we review You will not automatically lose Medicaid coverage on January 1, 2027, if your state adopts the federal hold-harmless option once CMS approves it, or if you qualify for a statutory exemption. Under federal guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), states adopting the transition relief may pause denials and terminations for community engagement noncompliance through June 30, 2027. Beneficiaries must still complete scheduled renewals and report qualifying hours or exemption circumstances to keep their files in good standing. You will not automatically lose Medicaid on January 1, 2027, for missing the community engagement benchmark, but your immediate protection depends directly on whether your state chooses to pause disenrollments. Under section 71119 of Public Law 119-21, often called the Working Families Tax Cut legislation, the federal baseline requires states to implement community engagement rules no later than January 1, 2027. However, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services ( CMS ) released State Medicaid Director Letter SMD# 26-006 on November 13, 2026, granting states an optional hold-harmless transition window. In a state that formally elects this hold-harmless period and has CMS approval, the Medicaid agency can suspend all eligibility denials and disenrollments based on community engagement noncompliance through June 30, 2027. This suspension applies to initial applications submitted and redetermination renewals initiated through that mid-year date. Even in participating states, administrators must still collect information and assess whether members meet the engagement rules. Enrollees must continue submitting paperwork, but coverage cannot be terminated strictly for failing the work requirement during this window. In states that do not adopt the hold-harmless policy, the federal requirement applies from January 1, 2027 unless the state has another CMS-approved mitigation, so ask your state Medicaid agency. If an individual in an enforcement state fails to demonstrate required hours or an exemption, the state agency cannot terminate benefits without warning. Federal regulations under the CMS Interim Final Rule (IFR) require the agency to send a formal noncompliance notice. Beneficiaries then receive a window of 30 calendar days to submit proof of qualifying activities or claim an exemption before disenrollment takes effect, as the CMS interim rule describes it. States implement the notice, and the Oct 29, 2026 court ruling partly vacated parts of that rule. Who the Rule Covers and Who Is Exempt The federal community engagement mandate applies strictly to non-pregnant adults ages 19 through 64 who are enrolled in the Medicaid expansion adult group or certain section 1115 minimum essential coverage demonstrations across 43 states and the District of Columbia. United States territories are not subject to the mandate, and individuals entitled to or enrolled in Medicare are excluded from these requirements. To satisfy the standard, covered adults must log at least 80 hours per month of qualifying activities or earn wages equal to at least 80 times the federal minimum wage, which equals $580 per month in 2026. Qualifying activities can be combined to reach the 80-hour monthly threshold. Approved activities include work, community service, a work program, or half-time education, or a combination. When checking compliance, state agencies review past records: applicants must demonstrate compliance for at least one month prior to application, while existing enrollees are checked across one or more months between redetermination cycles as determined by individual state rules. Federal policy provides explicit statutory exemptions that protect vulnerable groups from disenrollment. According to official CMS documentation, you are exempt from the 80-hour monthly rule if you meet any of the following criteria: * You are pregnant or postpartum. * You are a parent or primary caretaker responsible for a child age 13 or younger, or you care for an individual with a recognized disability. * You are a former foster youth. * You are an American Indian or Alaska Native individual. * You are a totally disabled veteran. * You are deemed medically frail. * You are in substance use disorder treatment. * You are currently complying with existing work requirements under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program or the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). * You are currently incarcerated in a correctional facility. If you qualify for any exemption, you must notify your state agency to ensure your administrative record is coded appropriately. What a Hold-Harmless State Can and Cannot Do State Medicaid Director Letter SMD# 26-006 establishes clear boundaries regarding state authority during the transition. A state that elects the hold-harmless option receives federal protection against CMS enforcement actions once CMS approves the period in its mitigation plan if it chooses to halt adverse eligibility decisions. Under this mechanism, the state Medicaid program can suspend both application denials and mid-year disenrollments for individuals who do not show compliance with community engagement standards. States have the flexibility to implement this relief for the entire period through June 30, 2027, or choose a shorter calendar duration that suits their technical rollout schedules. Electing the hold-harmless policy does not allow a state to pause normal Medicaid verification standards. States are expressly required to build reporting mechanisms, gather activity documentation, and evaluate whether applicants qualify for exemptions. States intending to use the hold-harmless option starting January 1, 2027, were asked by CMS to submit notifications by December 11, 2026, through their formal community engagement mitigation plans. The hold-harmless period applies only to community engagement standards under section 1902(xx)(1) of the Social Security Act and 42 CFR 435.559. A state may not suspend denials or disenrollments for other eligibility factors, such as age or household income. As verified on November 23, 2026, by the Oregon Health Authority (OHA), Oregon announced on Nov 23, 2026 that it will opt into the hold-harmless period, and it is the one state this page verified from a primary source. Other states may also opt in, so check your own state Medicaid agency. OHA said no Oregon Health Plan member will face coverage denials or disenrollment for community engagement noncompliance through June 30, 2027. Oregon state officials noted that more than 600,000 members received informational notices in September 2026, and Governor Tina Kotek's office said an initial analysis projected that up to a third of affected Oregonians would be likely to lose coverage even if they qualify. Implementation also occurs alongside ongoing legal developments: on October 29, 2026, the federal district court in Massachusetts v. Oz partially vacated specific CMS regulatory limits regarding medical condition exemptions, which CMS formally acknowledged in footnote three of SMD# 26-006. Ask your state Medicaid agency whether your state has adopted the hold harmless period and when it ends. Decide how you will document compliance before your next renewal. If you work, collect pay stubs, earnings statements or tax records showing at least $580 in gross monthly income or 80 logged hours. If you meet an exemption, gather your records now. Watch your mail for notices. In a state that has not delayed enforcement, a noncompliance notice gives you 30 calendar days to respond. Under federal statutory formulas, the baseline limit adjusts annually based on changes in the national average home price between the third quarter of the previous year and the third quarter of the current year. Between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026, average home prices increased by 2.72 percent, and FHFA applied that identical 2.72 percent rate of increase to the baseline loan threshold. In high-cost areas where local median home values exceed the national baseline, federal law establishes a local ceiling calculated at 150 percent of the baseline conforming limit. For one-unit properties in these high-cost counties, the 2027 ceiling is $1,283,100. Specific statutory exceptions apply to Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In those four designated regions, the local baseline limit is set at $1,283,100 and the maximum high-cost ceiling reaches $1,924,650 for a single-family one-unit residence. Conforming loan limits define the maximum dollar size of a mortgage that government-sponsored enterprises Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can acquire. These limits apply specifically to the total principal balance of the mortgage note, not to the contract purchase price of the real estate. When a buyer submits a down payment, the loan amount represents only the remaining unpaid balance. A homebuyer purchasing a property priced above $855,400 can still obtain a conforming loan as long as their cash down payment reduces the total borrowed principal to $855,400 or less. Using the mathematical formula of purchase price equal to loan limit divided by one minus the down payment share, we calculated the maximum transaction value supported by conforming loans at baseline and high-cost limits. Even for loans falling inside that $22,650 band, waiting until January does not guarantee conforming treatment without direct lender confirmation. FHFA states in its official documentation that conforming loan limits apply to mortgages acquired by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac in the 2027 calendar year. The agency's public data pages tie the limits to the calendar year in which the loan is acquired and do not state a specific loan delivery rule or origination date rule. Mortgage lenders establish their own pipeline policies regarding when they begin applying upcoming loan limits to newly originated applications. You must ask your lender directly which annual limit applies to your specific closing date. What Changes If You Go Jumbo A loan above the conforming limit in your county is a jumbo loan. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac cannot acquire it under the 2027 limit, so each lender sets its own underwriting rules and terms for it. A federal lawsuit led by New York and 20 other states plus the District of Columbia, joined by Pennsylvania's governor, is currently challenging the rule in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. Tools for this journey Rent Budget Planning Guide → On This Page What Changes on December 14 Who Is Affected and Which Programs Are Covered Timeline Table Timeline and Deadlines for Mixed-Status Families The Multistate Lawsuit Challenging the Rule What Tenants and Assisted Families Should Do Now Our Takeaway on HUD Verification Requirements What Changes on December 14 The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) published its final rule in the Federal Register on November 12, 2026, under document number FR 2026-23003 , titled Housing and Community Development Act of 1980: Verification of Eligible Status (91 FR 72978). This regulation carries an official effective date of December 14, 2026. The most consequential change in the regulation revises HUD's Section 214 rules by requiring verification of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status for every individual applicant and recipient of assistance under covered programs, regardless of how old the family member is. Under regulations that existed prior to this final rule, mixed-status families were permitted to live together in subsidized housing while receiving prorated assistance. In those arrangements, a household received a partial rent subsidy calculated strictly for the members who had verified citizenship or eligible immigration status, while members without eligible status received no direct subsidy. Under those prior standards, an individual family member could elect not to contend eligible status. Choosing that option meant the individual did not have to submit immigration documents, and the family simply accepted a smaller, prorated subsidy that reflected only the eligible members. The final rule published on November 12 completely eliminates that option. Going forward, every person living in an assisted unit must have their status affirmatively verified. Prorated assistance is no longer an ongoing arrangement that a family can maintain indefinitely. Instead, the final rule redefines prorated assistance as a temporary status that only applies while the verification of all household members is actively pending, where permitted by statute. If any member of the household cannot or does not establish eligible status, the family can no longer rely on long-term proration to maintain subsidized tenancy under covered housing programs. Who Is Affected and Which Programs Are Covered The reach of the regulation is defined by the underlying statutory authorities governing federal housing subsidies. According to HUD's official guidance and the Federal Register preamble, the final rule applies specifically to Section 214 covered programs. The covered programs include Section 236 of the National Housing Act, specifically for tenants paying below-market rent. They also include programs authorized under the United States Housing Act of 1937: Public Housing, the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) program, Project-based Section 8 rental assistance, and low-income units supported by Housing Development Grants. In contrast, HUD explicitly identifies several multifamily programs that are not covered by this Section 214 final rule. The excluded categories are Section 202 and Section 811 Project Rental Assistance Contracts (202/811 PRAC), Section 811 Project Rental Assistance (811 PRA), Senior Preservation Rental Assistance Contracts (SPRAC), and Section 202/162 Project Assistance Contracts (202/162 PAC). Households residing in units subsidized strictly under these excluded programs are not subject to the new verification mandate or the removal of the election not to contend eligible status. According to HUD estimates cited in the New York Attorney General's Nov 23, 2026 release , approximately 20,000 mixed-status families nationwide could lose their rental assistance under the new mandate. Those households encompass roughly 78,100 individual residents. Notably, the same estimates indicate that about 55,000 of the individuals who stand to lose assistance are fully eligible residents themselves, mostly children. The shortest timeline applies directly to mixed-status families who are already receiving assistance but have members who have not submitted verification evidence. For tenants in mixed families who have not submitted proof of citizenship or eligible immigration status as of December 14, 2026, the final rule requires that all required documentation be submitted within 90 days of December 14, 2026. That 90-day window sets the initial deadline at approximately March 14, 2027. For all other existing tenants in covered programs who have not previously submitted verification evidence, the timeline is longer. Those non-mixed households must submit proof at their next regular annual or interim reexamination of income and household composition scheduled after December 14, 2026. For applicants seeking admission to covered programs, verification documents must be submitted no later than the date when the housing provider examines other eligibility criteria. Housing providers and responsible entities have specific legal obligations during this rollout. Housing authorities and private property owners must deliver an official Section 214 notification to every tenant who has not yet submitted evidence no later than 30 days after the December 14 effective date. However, HUD specifically declined to tie the running of the 90-day compliance window to the date an individual tenant receives that letter. The 90-day clock runs strictly from the effective date of December 14, 2026. A tenant who cannot produce the necessary documents before the deadline may qualify for an extension. Under Section 5.508(g) of the rule, a housing authority or owner must grant an extension if the family submits the required declaration and consent forms certifying eligible status, certifies that the underlying documents are temporarily unavailable or more time is needed, and shows that prompt, diligent efforts will be made to obtain the evidence. Any extension granted under this provision must be issued in writing, cannot exceed 60 days in total, and cannot run concurrently with other submission timelines. The Multistate Lawsuit Challenging the Rule On November 23, 2026, a major legal challenge was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts seeking to invalidate HUD's final rule. The lawsuit is led by New York Attorney General Letitia James and represents a coalition of 22 attorneys general. The plaintiffs include New York and 20 other states plus the District of Columbia, joined by Pennsylvania's governor. The specific plaintiff states identified in the action are Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, alongside New York. The complaint asserts that HUD exceeded its statutory authority under the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980. The states argue that Congress explicitly codified the ability of mixed-status families to receive prorated housing assistance through legislation enacted in 1997, and that HUD lacks the administrative authority to overwrite that statutory compromise by regulation. Furthermore, the coalition argues that HUD violates the Administrative Procedure Act. The lawsuit asks the federal court to issue a declaration, vacatur, and an injunction for plaintiff states. However, tenants and advocates must recognize that as of November 25, 2026, no court order, temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction, or vacatur has been granted in the multistate case. The filing of a lawsuit does not pause a federal regulation. Unless and until a federal judge signs an order blocking the rule, housing providers remain legally bound to implement the December 14, 2026 requirements. What Tenants and Assisted Families Should Do Now Do not leave your home or give up your voucher because of rumors. The rule sets notice periods and extensions, and a pending lawsuit does not stop it on its own. Contact your housing authority or property owner to confirm which program funds your unit and which family members have already submitted documents. Gather identity and status documents for every household member. Ask about an extension. A housing provider must grant one of up to 60 days in total if you certify that eligible status exists and that the evidence is temporarily unavailable, and you show diligent efforts to get it. Contact local legal aid or a tenant advocacy group about your household's records and the lawsuit. If a subsidy change could affect your budget, plan with our guide on how much to spend on rent . Our Takeaway on HUD Verification Requirements If your household resides in Public Housing, uses a Housing Choice Voucher, or lives in Project-based Section 8 housing, you should start gathering documents now, because the rule takes effect December 14, 2026. Assemble proof of citizenship or eligible immigration status for every person listed on your lease. Mixed-status families should not wait for their annual renewal date, because the regulation sets a 90-day submission deadline measured from December 14, 2026, which falls on approximately March 14, 2027. Most other households have a year or more, since they submit at their next annual or interim reexamination. This recommendation is based on the published regulatory text in Federal Register document 2026-23003 and the current procedural status of the federal docket. Our guidance would change if the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts or another federal court enters an order staying the effective date or granting a preliminary injunction, or if HUD formally issues an administrative stay or revised implementation timeline. Until an official court order or housing authority notice confirms a delay, tenants should assume the verification deadlines remain fully operative. Frequently Asked Questions What happens if a family cannot provide documents before the 90-day deadline? If a mixed-status family cannot provide documentation within the 90-day window following December 14, 2026, the household can request a formal extension. Under Section 5.508(g) of the final rule, housing providers must grant an extension of up to 60 days if the family submits forms certifying that unverified members hold eligible status and explains in writing that documents are temporarily unavailable despite diligent efforts. If a family fails to submit documentation after the deadline and any granted extension, consequences follow under paragraph (h) of the rule. Does the multistate lawsuit stop the rule from taking effect on December 14? No. The filing of a federal complaint does not pause or block a federal regulation. A coalition of 22 attorneys general, led by New York and joined by Pennsylvania's governor, filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on November 23, 2026, seeking an injunction and vacatur. However, as of November 25, 2026, no court order or injunction has been issued. The rule remains scheduled to take effect on December 14, 2026, unless a judge issues a stay before that date. Can mixed-status families still elect not to contend eligible status? No. Under prior HUD regulations, family members could elect not to contend eligible immigration status, which allowed the household to receive prorated assistance without submitting immigration papers for those individuals. The final rule published on November 12, 2026, officially eliminates the election not to contend eligible status. Every member of an assisted household under covered programs must now have their eligible status verified. Are Section 202 and Section 811 housing programs affected by the rule? HUD's page lists the 202/811 PRAC, 811 PRA, SPRAC and 202/162 PAC programs as not covered. Public Housing, Housing Choice Vouchers and Project-based Section 8 are covered. Ask your housing authority or owner which program funds your unit. How will tenants be notified about the new verification requirements? The final rule requires responsible entities, such as local public housing authorities or private property owners participating in covered programs, to issue an official Section 214 notice to each tenant who has not yet submitted proof of citizenship or eligible status. This notice must be sent no later than 30 days after the December 14, 2026 effective date. However, the 90-day compliance period for mixed-status families runs from December 14, 2026, rather than the date the notice is received.
